slides.title: Is your Core Customer still right?
slides.support: In Metronome: open War Room. Read your Core Customer aloud. Is this still the customer you most want more of?
notes: Put the team’s own Core Customer on the screen. The example here is a reminder of its parts.
Ask: are their three needs still right, in the same order? What did the year teach you about them?
Choosing one Core Customer and ranking their three needs was the Q2 work. If it is missing, keep going and mark the result draft.
Change only what the evidence changes. The differentiators must serve these needs.
slides.headline: Is your Core Customer still right?

artwork.alt: An example Core Customer for the subscription company. Core Customer: owner of a small business. Description: the owner of a business with 10 to 50 staff. They decide alone, pay by card, and want it working this month without an IT person. Prioritized needs. 1, up and running in days. 2, a cost they can predict. 3, a person to call when stuck. Prioritized benefits. 1, active in 5 days or fewer. 2, one flat monthly price. 3, a named contact for 90 days. Persona: Dana, owner of a 20-person business. Revenue 55%, profit 60%.

slides.title: Is the line on your Attribution Map still right?
slides.support: In Metronome: open War Room. Put your Attribution Map on the screen. Is your 3HAG line still right?
notes: Put the team’s own Attribution Map on the screen. The example here is a reminder of its parts.
At Q3 the team drew its 3HAG line: where it will be in 3 years on each attribute. Read it: where it will lead, what it will maintain and what it will let drop.
Ask what has changed since the team drew it. Agree on the line now, for the new 3-year date.
At the first annual this is a review. From the second annual on, rebuild the map from scratch: attributes, scores and line.
If the line is not agreed or the competitors are not scored, keep going and mark the result draft.
slides.headline: Is the line on your Attribution Map still right?

artwork.alt: A line graph for the subscription company. Twelve market attributes run along the bottom, ordered from the one the company serves best. They start with speed of setup, ease of use, price predictability, reliability, billing simplicity and support from a person. Security, integrations, reporting, feature breadth, customization and partner network follow. Scores run from 1 to 5. Five lines: Us today, Competitor A, Competitor B, Competitor C and the 3HAG line. Us today runs from 4 on the left to 2 on the right. The 3HAG line rises to 5 on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person. It drops on reporting and customization.
